1099.def: Work where you're paid as your own boss, like gig or delivery apps. No taxes are taken out, so it's smart to set some money aside for tax time.

401k.def: A retirement savings account you get through your job. Money comes out of your paycheck before you see it, and it grows for later.

401k-match.def: Extra money your job adds to your 401(k) when you save. For example, if you save $50, your job might add $50 too. It's like a raise.

andon.def: A pause button. In a factory, anyone can stop the line when something's wrong. On this site, it means it's OK to pause your money plan when life happens.

apr.def: The yearly cost of borrowing money, shown as a percent. A 24.9% APR means about $249 a year in interest for every $1,000 you owe.

bond-fund.def: A basket of loans to governments or companies. They pay you interest. They usually go up and down less than stocks, and usually grow less too.

catch-up-contribution.def: Extra money people age 50 and older are allowed to put into retirement accounts each year, on top of the normal limit.

check-casher.def: A store that turns your paycheck into cash for a fee. The fees add up fast. A free bank or credit union account can do the same thing for free.

compound-growth.def: When your money earns money, and then that new money earns money too. Over many years, this snowball does most of the work.

credit-union.def: A bank owned by its members instead of investors. Many have lower fees. Look for NCUA insurance, which protects your money like FDIC does.

diversification.def: Not putting all your eggs in one basket. Owning many different things means one bad one can't sink everything.

emergency-fund.def: Money saved just for surprises, like a car repair or a doctor bill, so you don't have to borrow. Some people call it a cushion.

expense-ratio.def: The yearly fee a fund charges, shown as a percent. A 0.05% expense ratio costs 50 cents a year for every $1,000 you have in it.

fdic.def: A U.S. government agency that protects money in member banks, up to $250,000 per person per bank. If the bank fails, you still get your money back.

index-fund.def: A basket that holds small pieces of many companies at once, like the 500 biggest U.S. companies. It usually has low fees.

ira.def: A retirement account you open on your own, not through a job. It has tax benefits to help your money grow for later.

jidoka.def: A safety gate. In a factory, work stops if something isn't right. On this site, it means you don't move to the next money step until the one you're on is safe.

kaizen.def: Small, steady improvements. On this site, it means tiny regular money steps, like saving $5 a week, that add up over time.

market-drop.def: When prices of investments fall for a while. It happens often and is a normal part of investing. Prices have recovered over time in the past, but not always quickly.

paper-trading.def: A pretend investing account with fake money. You can learn how things work and how a drop feels, without any real risk.

roth-ira.def: A type of IRA where you pay taxes on the money now. Later, in retirement, you can usually take it out tax-free.

secure-2.def: A 2022 U.S. law that changed retirement rules. One change: people 50 and older can save extra each year in 401(k)s and IRAs.

single-stock.def: A small piece of one company. If that one company does badly, your money can drop a lot. That's why it's riskier than a fund.

social-security.def: Monthly money from the U.S. government after you retire, based on your work history. Waiting longer to start it usually means a bigger monthly check.

overdraft.def: A fee a bank charges when you spend more than you have in your account. It's often about $35. Some accounts have no overdraft fees.

active-fund.def: A fund where people pick which investments to buy. It usually charges higher fees than an index fund, and often doesn't do better.

share.def: One small piece of a company or fund. If you own 2 shares and the price goes up $1, your shares are worth $2 more.

ticker.def: A short code for a stock or fund, like AAPL for Apple. You use it to look up the price.

market-order.def: An order to buy or sell right away at the current price, whatever it is at that moment.

apy.def: Annual Percentage Yield: how much a savings account pays in a year, as a percent. 4% APY on $1,000 is about $40 a year.

high-yield-savings.def: A savings account that pays much more interest than a regular one, often at an online bank or credit union. Look for FDIC or NCUA insurance.

profit-loss.def: How much more (profit) or less (loss) your investments are worth than what you paid. It is only real when you sell.
